question: How do I hire a fractional CRO in Charleston?
body:
## Direct Answer
To hire a fractional CRO in Charleston, define the revenue problem you need solved, decide whether you truly need a Chief Revenue Officer versus a VP of Sales, then source candidates through fractional-executive networks, RevOps communities, and local Charleston founder circles. Vet them on outcomes rather than logos, structure a 3-to-6-month scoped engagement with clear exit criteria, and measure against a written scorecard from week one.

Hiring a fractional Chief Revenue Officer is one of the highest-leverage moves a Charleston company can make when it is stuck between "founder-led sales" and "we can't yet justify a $300K+ full-time revenue executive." The fractional model gives you senior go-to-market leadership for a fraction of the week and a fraction of the cost — but only if you scope it correctly, vet ruthlessly, and hold the engagement to measurable outcomes. The sections below walk through exactly how to do that, from deciding whether you even need a CRO to onboarding one and knowing when to graduate them out.

## What does a fractional CRO actually do, and how is it different from a consultant?
A fractional CRO is a senior revenue leader who owns your go-to-market outcomes on a part-time, ongoing basis — typically one to three days a week — rather than advising from the sidelines. Unlike a consultant who delivers a deck and leaves, a fractional CRO carries a number. They sit in your pipeline reviews, coach your reps, sign off on comp plans, and are accountable for the same revenue targets a full-time CRO would own. The "fractional" part refers to time and cost, not to depth of ownership.

In practice, the mandate spans the entire revenue engine: sales, marketing alignment, RevOps, pricing, forecasting, and often customer success or renewals. A strong fractional CRO in a market like Charleston will spend their first weeks diagnosing where revenue actually leaks — is it a lead-generation problem, a conversion problem, a retention problem, or a forecasting problem? — before touching anything. The distinction matters because many founders assume they have a "sales problem" when the real issue is an unrepeatable motion or a broken handoff between marketing and sales. A good operator refuses to prescribe before they diagnose, and that discipline is what separates a fractional CRO from an expensive advisor. For a deeper breakdown of the role's scope, see [pulserevops.com/knowledge/cro-role-scope](https://pulserevops.com/knowledge/cro-role-scope).

The other thing a fractional CRO brings is pattern recognition. Because they've built revenue engines across many companies, they've seen the failure modes before — the pipeline that looks healthy but is stuffed with dead deals, the comp plan that quietly incentivizes discounting, the "great" rep who is actually the only one who can sell. That outside perspective is exactly what a founder who has only run one company cannot generate internally, and it is the single biggest reason the model works.

## When does a Charleston company actually need a fractional CRO instead of a full-time hire?
The honest answer is: less often than you'd think, and at very specific inflection points. A fractional CRO is the right call when your revenue is stalled or scaling faster than your leadership can handle, you don't yet have a repeatable sales motion, and you can't justify — or attract — a full-time revenue executive. That's typically a company somewhere between roughly $1M and $15M in revenue: past the founder-led-sales stage, but not yet at the scale where a full-time CRO's comp is a rounding error.

The decision comes down to three questions: Do you have a repeatable go-to-market motion? Can you afford full-time executive compensation? And is the problem a build problem or a run problem? Fractional CROs excel at the build — installing the process, the metrics discipline, the hiring playbook — and then handing off to a VP of Sales or a full-time CRO to run it. If you already have a working machine and just need someone to operate it day-to-day, you probably want a full-time hire, not a fractional one.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  A[Revenue stalled or scaling fast] --> B{Do you have a repeatable sales motion}
  B -->|No| C[Fractional CRO builds the motion]
  B -->|Yes| D{Can you afford full time comp}
  D -->|No| C
  D -->|Yes| E[Hire full time CRO]
  C --> F[Three to six month roadmap]
  F --> G[Handoff to VP Sales or full time CRO]
```

Charleston adds a specific wrinkle worth naming. The local talent pool for senior SaaS and B2B revenue leaders is thinner than in Atlanta, Austin, or the Bay Area, which means a full-time CRO search can drag on for six-plus months and often ends in an expensive relocation package. The fractional model sidesteps that entirely — many fractional CROs work remotely or split time across the Southeast, so you get senior talent without competing for a scarce local full-time hire. For companies weighing the trade-off, the calculus is often "a proven fractional operator this quarter" versus "maybe a full-time hire two quarters from now." When speed matters, fractional usually wins.

## Where do you find qualified fractional CROs who know the Charleston and Southeast market?
Sourcing is where most first-time hires go wrong — they either post a job listing (which attracts full-time seekers, not fractional operators) or ask their VC for "someone good" and take the first warm intro. The better approach is to fish in the ponds where fractional executives actually swim. Fractional-executive marketplaces and talent networks — platforms built specifically to match part-time senior operators with companies — are the most direct channel, because everyone on them is explicitly offering fractional work.

Beyond the marketplaces, the highest-signal sources are peer referrals and community. Charleston has a genuine and growing startup and small-business ecosystem — the Harbor Entrepreneur Center, Charleston Digital Corridor, and the broader SEED SC and Charleston Angel network — and founders in those circles have often already hired or interviewed fractional revenue leaders. A warm referral from a founder who has actually worked with someone is worth ten cold marketplace profiles, because it comes with an implicit reference check. RevOps and go-to-market communities online (Pavilion, RevGenius, Wizards of Ops) are another strong channel, since they're full of the exact operators you want. See [pulserevops.com/knowledge/sourcing-revenue-leaders](https://pulserevops.com/knowledge/sourcing-revenue-leaders) for a fuller sourcing playbook.

One caution on the "Charleston" qualifier: do not over-index on local presence. A fractional CRO does not need to live in Charleston to serve a Charleston company well — the role is increasingly remote-first, and the pool of great operators who happen to live within driving distance of the peninsula is small. What matters far more is relevant domain fit: have they built revenue engines in your business model (B2B SaaS vs. services vs. e-commerce), at your stage, and in your motion (inbound, outbound, channel, product-led)? A remote operator who has scaled three companies exactly like yours will beat a local one who hasn't every time. Reserve the "local" preference for cases where in-person coaching of your sales floor is genuinely non-negotiable.

## How do you vet and interview a fractional CRO so you don't hire an expensive talker?
Vetting a fractional CRO is fundamentally different from vetting a full-time exec, because you're buying outcomes over a short window, not a multi-year cultural fit. The core principle: interview for evidence of building, not for polish. Fractional operators are, almost by definition, good at pitching themselves — that's part of the job. Your job is to get underneath the pitch to the specific, verifiable things they've actually done.

Ask outcome-anchored questions that force specificity. Instead of "How would you fix our pipeline?" ask "Walk me through the last time you inherited a broken forecast — what did you find, what did you change in the first 30 days, and what was the number six months later?" Then push on the details: What was the pipeline coverage ratio before and after? How did they change the comp plan and what did reps say? What did they get wrong? An operator who has genuinely done the work answers in concrete, slightly messy specifics. Someone who has mostly advised answers in frameworks and abstractions. That contrast is your single best signal.

Reference checks matter more here than almost anywhere, and you should insist on talking to a founder or CEO who worked with them — not just a peer. Ask the reference the killer question: "Would you hire them again, and for what specifically?" A hesitation or a narrowly-scoped answer ("They were great for the first 90 days but...") tells you exactly where the limits are. Finally, run a paid pilot diagnostic before committing to a longer engagement. Two weeks and a defined deliverable — a revenue diagnostic and a 90-day plan — costs little, and how they perform in that window is far more predictive than any interview. For the interview scorecard framework, see [pulserevops.com/knowledge/vetting-fractional-execs](https://pulserevops.com/knowledge/vetting-fractional-execs).

## How are fractional CRO engagements structured and priced without getting burned?
Engagements typically run on a monthly retainer tied to a defined time commitment — commonly one to three days a week — with a fixed initial term of three to six months and clear renewal or graduation criteria. The exact rate varies widely by the operator's seniority, your stage, and the scope, so treat any single number you hear as a starting point rather than a market rate; the important thing is that pricing maps to a defined time commitment and defined outcomes, not to a vague "advisory" arrangement. Avoid open-ended, indefinite retainers with no exit criteria — that's how a fractional engagement quietly becomes an overpriced permanent fixture that nobody is accountable for.

Structure the engagement in phases rather than as one undifferentiated retainer. A clean structure looks like: a short scoping and diagnostic phase, a written 90-day plan, an execution-and-coaching phase, and a monthly scorecard review that gates renewal. Tie some portion of the arrangement to milestones where it makes sense — but be careful with heavy variable/equity comp on short fractional engagements, because it can distort incentives toward short-term wins over durable ones. The cleanest arrangements pair a fair fixed retainer with a genuinely honest monthly review of whether the work is moving the number.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  A[Scoping call] --> B[Diagnostic audit]
  B --> C[Ninety day plan]
  C --> D[Execution and coaching]
  D --> E[Monthly scorecard review]
  E --> F[Renew or graduate]
```

Two contract details protect you. First, define the deliverables and the day-count in writing — "up to two days per week, focused on pipeline, forecasting, and sales coaching" — so scope creep in either direction is visible. Second, build in a clean off-ramp: a 30-day notice period on both sides and an explicit graduation clause. The best possible outcome of a fractional CRO engagement is that they work themselves out of a job by building a machine and a full-time leader to run it. A contract that assumes and plans for that graduation is healthier than one structured to maximize the retainer's lifespan.

## How do you onboard a fractional CRO and measure whether it's working?
Onboarding a fractional operator is a race against the clock — you're paying for one to three days a week, so every day spent lost in your systems is expensive. Front-load access and context: get them into your CRM, your dashboards, your last four quarters of pipeline data, your comp plans, and a handful of recorded sales calls before day one. The faster they can see the raw truth of your revenue engine, the faster the diagnosis. A good fractional CRO will ask for exactly this; if they don't, that's a yellow flag.

Measurement is where discipline pays off. Agree on a written scorecard in the first two weeks — a short list of the metrics that define success for this engagement. Depending on the problem, that's some combination of pipeline coverage ratio, win rate, sales-cycle length, forecast accuracy, ramp time for new reps, and net revenue retention. The point is not to track everything; it's to name the three-to-five numbers that this person is being hired to move, agree on the baseline, and review them monthly against the trend. Leading indicators (activity, pipeline created, coverage) matter as much as lagging ones (closed revenue) early on, because revenue lags the work by a quarter or two.

Finally, watch the intangibles that a scorecard won't catch. Is your sales team more confident and better coached, or more anxious? Are your pipeline reviews sharper and more honest? Is your forecast something you now trust? A fractional CRO's real work often shows up first in the quality of your revenue conversations and only later in the revenue itself. If the operator is building durable capability — installing process, upgrading your people, documenting the playbook — you're getting your money's worth even before the number moves. If three months in you've gotten a lot of activity but no clearer system and no capability transfer, that's your signal to have the hard conversation before you renew.

## Related questions
### What's the difference between a fractional CRO and a fractional VP of Sales?
A fractional CRO owns the entire revenue engine — sales, marketing alignment, RevOps, pricing, retention — while a fractional VP of Sales owns execution of the sales motion specifically. Choose CRO for strategy and system-building, VP of Sales for running an existing motion.

### How much does a fractional CRO cost?
Pricing is a monthly retainer tied to a defined time commitment (often one to three days a week) and varies widely by seniority, stage, and scope. Don't anchor on a single quoted number — anchor on cost-per-defined-outcome and compare against a full-time exec's fully-loaded comp.

### Can a fractional CRO work remotely for a Charleston company?
Yes, and most do. The role is increasingly remote-first, which is an advantage given Charleston's relatively thin local pool of senior revenue executives. Prioritize domain and stage fit over physical proximity unless in-person sales-floor coaching is essential.

### How long should a fractional CRO engagement last?
Typically three to six months for the build phase, with monthly reviews gating renewal. The ideal endpoint is graduation — the fractional CRO installs the system and hands off to a full-time leader or VP of Sales they've helped you hire.

### Do early-stage startups need a fractional CRO?
Usually not before roughly $1M in revenue. Before that, founder-led sales is still the best teacher and the fastest feedback loop. A fractional CRO earns their keep once you have some traction to systematize but can't yet justify a full-time revenue executive.

## FAQ
**What size company is a fractional CRO right for?**
Generally companies between roughly $1M and $15M in revenue that have moved past founder-led sales but can't yet justify a full-time CRO. Below that, focus on founder-led selling; above it, you likely need a full-time leader.

**Should I hire locally in Charleston or is remote fine?**
Remote is fine and often better. Charleston's local pool of senior revenue executives is limited, so restricting your search geographically can cost you the best operators. Weight domain and stage fit far above location.

**How do I know if I need a CRO versus fixing sales myself?**
If you can't articulate a repeatable, documented sales motion — how leads become pipeline become revenue with predictable conversion rates — you likely need outside senior help. If you have the motion and just need more reps, you need hiring, not a CRO.

**What should the first 90 days look like?**
Diagnostic audit first, then a written 90-day plan with a scorecard, then execution and coaching. Be skeptical of anyone who prescribes fixes before diagnosing your actual revenue leaks.

**How do I avoid hiring an expensive advisor who doesn't own outcomes?**
Insist on ownership of a number, a written scorecard, and a paid two-week pilot diagnostic before a longer commitment. Interview for specific past outcomes, not frameworks, and check references with founders they've actually worked for.

**Can a fractional CRO help me hire my eventual full-time CRO?**
Yes — this is one of the best uses of the role. A strong fractional operator builds the revenue system, defines the role, and helps you recruit and onboard the full-time leader who will run it, then graduates out cleanly.

**What red flags should I watch for during vetting?**
Prescribing before diagnosing, answering in abstractions rather than specifics, no founder-level references, resistance to a scoped pilot, and contract structures with no exit criteria or graduation clause. Any of these warrants a hard second look.

**How do I measure ROI on a fractional CRO?**
Track three-to-five agreed metrics against a baseline — pipeline coverage, win rate, sales-cycle length, forecast accuracy, retention — plus capability transfer: is your team better coached and is your revenue system more durable than before?
